title: How much is it?
goal: Count to ten thousand, give prices in 塊, and haggle at a night market — while settling the 二 vs 兩 question that trips up every beginner.
bekal: count and read prices up to five digits
use 兩 before measure words and 二 for counting
haggle at a 夜市 with the sentences Taiwanese people actually use

dialogs.title: 對話 — 士林夜市
dialogs.intro: Saturday night at the Shilin night market. Budi wants to buy a T-shirt, and Xiaomei comes along to help him haggle.

lines.speaker: 老闆:
lines.text: [來來來|Lái lái lái]！[看一下|Kàn yíxià]！[很便宜|Hěn piányí]！
lines.id: Come on in! Have a look! Really cheap!

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.id: Excuse me, how much is this?

lines.speaker: 老闆:
lines.id: Three fifty. Pure cotton, you know!

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.id: Three fifty? That's a bit pricey.

lines.speaker: 小美:
lines.text: [老闆|Lǎobǎn]，[算|suàn][便宜|piányí][一點|yìdiǎn][啦|la]！[我們|Wǒmen][買|mǎi][兩件|liǎng jiàn]。
lines.id: Come on, a little cheaper! We're buying two.
lines.literal: boss, count — cheap — a-little — (la)! we — buy — two — (measure word).

lines.speaker: 老闆:
lines.text: [兩件|Liǎng jiàn][的話|de huà]，[六百|liùbǎi][好不好|hǎo bù hǎo]？
lines.id: For two, how about six hundred?
lines.literal: two — (measure word) — (if), six-hundred — good — not — good?

lines.speaker: 小美:
lines.id: Five fifty! We're students, you know.

lines.speaker: 老闆:
lines.text: [哎唷|Āiyō]…[好啦|Hǎo la]！[五百八|Wǔbǎi bā]，[不能|bù néng][再少|zài shǎo][了|le]。
lines.id: Oh man… fine! Five eighty, and I can't go any lower.
lines.literal: aiyo… good — (la)! five-hundred-eight, not — can — again — less — (now).

lines.speaker: 老闆:
lines.literal: thank thank! want — swipe-card — or — pay-cash?

lines.speaker: 老闆:
lines.id: Four twenty is your change. Thanks for coming!
lines.literal: find-back — you — four-hundred-two. thank thank — light-come!

lines.speaker: 小美:
lines.id: At a night market, you've got to haggle!
lines.literal: at — night-market — sure — must — cut-price — (you know)!

notes: ⚠️ **三百五 means 350, not 305.** When giving prices, a final round tens digit can be clipped: 三百五 = 三百五十, 五百八 = 五百八十, 四百二 = 四百二十. If you hear 三百五 and think 305, you'll pay the wrong amount.
**塊 (*kuài*) is the word people actually say**, while 元 (*yuán*) is what's printed on the receipt. Often both are dropped: just *三百五*. Compare "bucks" and "dollars" in English.
**還是 = "or" in questions**, 或是/或者 = "or" in statements. ⚠️ *你要茶還是咖啡？* (Tea or coffee?) is right; *你要茶或是咖啡？* sounds wrong.
**謝謝光臨** ("thank you for coming") is what shop staff say to customers as they leave. In a 便利商店 you'll hear it hundreds of times. You don't need to reply — a nod is enough.
⚠️ **妳 with the 女 component is "you" for a woman.** It sounds exactly the same: *nǐ*. Taiwan still uses this written distinction, along with 他 (he) and 她 (she), both also read *tā*.

grammars.title: ⚠️ 二 or 兩: a one-sentence rule
body: Mandarin has two words for the number two, and picking the wrong one is the beginner mistake you hear most often. The rule is short: **兩 before a measure word, 二 everywhere else.**
after: ⚠️ **兩個人** is right; **二個人** is wrong and sounds odd at once. Conversely **十二** is right; **十兩** is wrong. Quick test: if a measure word follows, use 兩.

**Clock times are an exception to memorize**: two o'clock is **兩點** (*liǎng diǎn*), because 點 is a measure word. But two minutes is **兩分**… and the second of the month is **二號**. Three forms, three rules.

grammars.title: Numbers and prices: 萬 changes how you count
body: Up to a thousand, Mandarin counts much like English. The difference starts at ten thousand.
after: ⚠️ **零 (*líng*) must be used to mark a gap inside a number**, and only once, however many zeros there are: 1005 = 一千零五, 1050 = 一千零五十.
**Everyday prices in Taiwan** as a yardstick: a 便利商店 coffee about 45 塊, a 便當 lunch box about 90 塊, one 捷運 ride 20–40 塊, a 珍珠奶茶 about 60 塊, a student room 5,000–9,000 塊 a month.

sections.title: Shopping: the sentences people really use

blocks.text: ⚠️ **打折 works the opposite way from what English speakers expect.** *八折* (*bā zhé*) is not eighty percent off but **paying eighty percent** — so the discount is twenty percent. *五折* = half price. A sign saying 三折 means you pay only thirty percent; that's a huge sale.

sections.title: Haggling: where you can and where you can't

blocks.title: ⚠️ Taiwan's unwritten rules
items: **You can haggle:** at night markets 夜市, traditional markets 傳統市場, small clothing and accessory shops, roadside fruit sellers.
**You can't haggle:** at 便利商店, chain stores, restaurants, pharmacies, department stores, ticket machines. Haggling at 7-Eleven will confuse the cashier, not offend them.
**The most natural opener:** *算便宜一點啦！* — rather than naming a number first. Let the seller come down.
**Trump cards that really work:** buying more than one (*我買兩件*) and saying you're students (*我們是學生耶*).
**When the price can't go lower, the seller will say** *不能再少了* or *真的沒賺錢*. That's your signal to stop; pushing further is considered rude.

blocks.text: Your tone matters far more than your words. Haggling in Taiwan is done with a smile, with 啦 and 耶 at the end of sentences, like joking with a friend. Haggling with a stern face changes the mood and actually gets you a worse price.

**色 means "color" and can be dropped** when 的 follows: *紅的* = "the red one". Clothing sizes use the English letters as they are, or: 大號 (L), 中號 (M), 小號 (S). To try something on: **我可以試穿嗎？** *Wǒ kěyǐ shìchuān ma?*
